pool.prompt: On a shared utility pole, where does fiber optic cable typically attach relative to electric power lines?
choices: At the very top — fiber gets priority because it is more sensitive to interference
In the supply space alongside primary power conductors
In the communication space — below the climbing space, below the primary power conductors and the neutral
Directly below the primary conductors with no required separation
pool.explanation: Fiber is a telecom cable and attaches in the communication space, the lowest zone on a shared pole. Supply (power) lines occupy the top zone. A mandatory climbing space separates the two zones so linemen can climb without their body bridging high-voltage and telecom equipment.
pool.citation: NESC C2-2023 (general clearance/space-separation rules for shared poles — see T01.md research log for verification scope).

pool.prompt: A cable is attached to a pole at 24 feet above the ground and sags to 20 feet above the ground at midspan. Where is ground clearance measured for compliance purposes?
choices: At the attachment point on the pole (24 feet)
At midspan — the lowest point of the sag (20 feet in this example)
At the halfway point between attachment height and sag height
Ground clearance is not measured for telecom cable, only for power lines
pool.explanation: Ground clearance is measured at midspan — the lowest point of the cable's sag — not at the attachment height on the pole. This is why crews must always clarify whether a stated height is "attachment height" or "midspan clearance"; they are different numbers, and only the midspan number determines compliance with minimum clearance rules over roads and other surfaces.
pool.citation: NESC C2-2023 (clearance measurement convention — exact rule/table number not independently verified this session; verify against the adopted edition before design lock).

pool.prompt: What is the name of the mandatory clearance zone between the supply space and communication space on a shared utility pole — a gap where nothing is attached, reserved so linemen can safely climb without bridging the two zones?
choices: Communication space
Climbing space
Supply space
Neutral zone
pool.explanation: Climbing space is a mandatory clearance zone — nothing is attached in it. It exists purely so a lineman climbing the pole never has their body bridging the gap between high-voltage supply conductors and telecom equipment. Violating climbing-space requirements is a serious compliance failure that endangers anyone who climbs that pole.
pool.citation: NESC C2-2023 (climbing-space requirement — document-level verified; exact rule number not independently confirmed, see T01.md).

pool.prompt: Who typically OWNS the utility poles that fiber companies attach to in most US markets, and under what FCC rule are the attachment fees set?
choices: The fiber company owns the pole; no FCC rule applies
The electric utility owns the pole; fiber companies pay annual attachment fees set under 47 CFR 1.1409 (the pole attachment rate formula)
Local government owns the pole as public infrastructure; fees are set by BICSI
The electric utility owns the pole; fees are set under 47 CFR 1.1411 (the pole-access application timeline rule)
pool.explanation: In most US markets the electric utility owns the pole, and fiber companies are "attachers" who pay annual attachment fees. The core rate formula lives in 47 CFR 1.1406; 47 CFR 1.1409 governs a specific cost-apportionment input that feeds into that formula. (47 CFR 1.1411 governs the *timeline* for a utility to process a pole-access application — a procedural rule, not the fee-setting rule; do not cite 1.1411 for attachment fees.)
pool.citation: 47 CFR 1.1406 (pole attachment rate formula); 47 CFR 1.1409 (cost-apportionment input); contrast with 47 CFR 1.1411 (application/survey timeline — see T01.md research log for the correction).

pool.prompt: What does RUS Bulletin 1751F-630 ("Design of Aerial Plant") govern that is directly relevant to pole work?
choices: Indoor fiber patch panel labeling conventions
Design requirements for RUS-funded aerial construction — including pole attachment, sag, and clearance design
FCC pole attachment rate calculations
Buried cable trenching depth only
pool.explanation: 1751F-630 is RUS's aerial-plant design bulletin, issued to RUS telecommunications borrowers through the Outside Plant Branch. For RUS-funded projects, it is the governing reference for aerial construction design choices — how poles, attachments, sag, and clearance are engineered — not for FCC rate-setting or indoor work.

pool.prompt: A wood pole's class (strength rating) is determined by measuring its circumference at what point?
choices: At the very top of the pole
6 feet from the butt (bottom) of the pole
At the midpoint of the pole's total length
At the ground line only, regardless of setting depth
pool.explanation: ANSI O5.1 determines a wood pole's true class by measuring its circumference 6 feet from the butt — the setting-depth reference point. Class 1 is the strongest common class; class numbers increase as strength decreases, with H1-H6 reserved for extra-heavy loads.
pool.citation: ANSI O5.1 (Wood Poles — Specifications and Dimensions) — Table 8M classification method.

pool.prompt: Match each vertical zone on a shared utility pole to what occupies it.

items.label: Nothing — mandatory open gap for linemen

pool.explanation: A shared pole is divided top-to-bottom: supply space (high-voltage power, licensed electricians only), climbing space (a mandatory empty gap for safe climbing), and communication space (telecom cables, where fiber attaches, typically at the bottom).
pool.citation: NESC C2-2023 (pole zone structure — document-level verified).

pool.prompt: In RUS-program areas, the neutral conductor at a pole is often also the MGN. What does MGN stand for, and why does it matter to a fiber crew?
choices: Main Ground Node — it has no bearing on fiber work
Multi-Grounded Neutral — grounded at every pole; fiber messenger wires must maintain NESC clearance from it and, in some areas, bond to it under specific requirements
Metallic Grounding Network — used only for electric transmission lines, never distribution
Modular Ground Nexus — a term specific to ADSS cable installations only
pool.explanation: MGN (Multi-Grounded Neutral) is the electric distribution system's return conductor, grounded at every pole in many RUS-program areas. Fiber messenger wires must maintain NESC-specified clearance from the neutral, and bonding the messenger to the neutral/MGN has specific grounding requirements a crew must follow.
pool.citation: RUS Bulletin 1751F-630 (RUS-area MGN bonding context for aerial plant).
